title: Is it healthy to eat eggs every day?

seo.title: Is it healthy to eat eggs every day?
seo.meta_description: For healthy people, up to one whole egg per day can fit a heart-healthy diet. Current AHA guidance emphasizes the overall pattern and saturated fat more than dietary cholesterol alone.
seo.search_intent: Understand whether one egg a day is healthy and when dietary cholesterol becomes more important.

excerpt: For healthy people, up to one whole egg per day can fit a heart-healthy dietary pattern. A large egg provides about 6–7 g protein and roughly 70–80 calories, plus close to 200 mg dietary cholesterol. Current American Heart Association guidance emphasizes the overall dietary pattern and saturated fat rather than treating dietary cholesterol as the primary cardiovascular target for most people.
content_html:
Eggs are nutrient-dense, but the useful question is not whether they are simply “good” or “bad.” It is how they fit into the whole diet. The American Heart Association's dietary-cholesterol advisory says healthy individuals can include up to one whole egg per day, while its 2026 cardiovascular dietary guidance puts the larger emphasis on the overall eating pattern.

What one egg provides

A large egg contains roughly 70–80 calories, 6–7 g protein, and 4–5 g fat. It also provides vitamin B12, choline, selenium, and other nutrients.

The yolk contains essentially all of the egg's fat and cholesterol as well as many of its vitamins and minerals. The white is mostly water and protein.

Dietary cholesterol is only part of the LDL story

A large egg contains close to 200 mg dietary cholesterol. The AHA's 2026 guidance notes that dietary cholesterol is no longer a primary cardiovascular target for most people; the broader pattern, including replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats, is more useful for risk reduction.

That does not make dietary cholesterol irrelevant for everyone. Individual responses and clinical circumstances vary, especially when LDL cholesterol is elevated.

What comes with the egg matters

An egg eaten with vegetables, whole grains, and unsaturated fats sits in a very different dietary pattern from eggs routinely paired with bacon, sausage, butter, and other foods rich in saturated fat.

This is why focusing on the egg count alone can miss the larger nutritional difference between two breakfasts that both contain one egg.

One per day is not a universal prescription

The AHA's dietary-cholesterol advisory allows up to one whole egg daily for healthy individuals, with caveats for people with dyslipidemia and certain cardiovascular risks. “Can fit” also does not mean everyone needs an egg every day.

If LDL cholesterol is high or cardiovascular risk is a concern, the appropriate amount should be considered alongside saturated fat, dietary cholesterol, medications, and the overall diet rather than copied from a population-level number.

Egg whites change the equation

Egg whites provide protein without the yolk's dietary cholesterol. Combining one whole egg with extra whites is one way to raise protein while keeping cholesterol intake lower, although the extra whites do not replace the yolk's micronutrients.

The practical rule

For a healthy adult, one whole egg per day can fit within a heart-healthy pattern. The more current framing is not to treat that number as a magic threshold: prioritize a diet rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, and unsaturated oils, and individualize the choice when LDL or cardiovascular risk is elevated.

faq.question: Is one egg a day healthy?
faq.answer: For healthy individuals, the American Heart Association's dietary-cholesterol advisory says up to one whole egg per day can fit a healthy dietary pattern.

faq.question: How much cholesterol is in an egg?
faq.answer: A large whole egg contains roughly 180–200 mg dietary cholesterol, concentrated in the yolk.

faq.question: Does current heart-health guidance focus mainly on egg cholesterol?
faq.answer: No. The AHA's 2026 dietary guidance emphasizes the overall dietary pattern and says dietary cholesterol is no longer a primary cardiovascular target for most people.
